questions.question_text: In which of the following pairs are the two vectors parallel?

options.why: The first components give $k=3$, but the second components give $\frac{26}{8}=3.25$; only one component was checked.
The components have been swapped, which does not produce a scalar multiple.
Swapping the components and changing one sign gives a perpendicular vector, not a parallel one.

questions.solution_text:
$\frac{9}{3}=3$
$\frac{24}{8}=3$
The same scalar works in both components, so $\begin{pmatrix}9\\24\end{pmatrix}=3\begin{pmatrix}3\\8\end{pmatrix}$ and this pair is parallel.

questions.question_text: Find the value of $t$ for which $\begin{pmatrix}-5\\8\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}20\\t\end{pmatrix}$ are parallel.

options.why: Used $k=4$ instead of $k=-4$, dropping the sign change.
Used the reciprocal scalar $-\frac{1}{4}$ and multiplied $8$ by it.
Added the first-component difference $20-(-5)=25$ to $8$ instead of multiplying by the scalar.

questions.question_text: Find the value of $w$ for which $\begin{pmatrix}6\\-9\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}-10\\w\end{pmatrix}$ are parallel.

options.why: Found the correct size but applied $k=\frac{5}{3}$ instead of $k=-\frac{5}{3}$.
Used the difference between the first components, $-10-6=-16$, and added it to $-9$ instead of using the ratio.
Used the difference between the first components rather than their ratio, and also dropped the sign.

questions.question_text:
The vectors below are written in terms of non-parallel, non-zero vectors $\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}$.
In which pair are the two vectors parallel?

options.why: The $\underset{\sim}{a}$ terms give $k=3$ but the $\underset{\sim}{b}$ terms give $k=2$; only one term was checked.
The coefficients have been swapped, which does not give a scalar multiple.
The $\underset{\sim}{a}$ terms give $k=2$ but the $\underset{\sim}{b}$ terms give $k=-2$; the sign was not carried.

questions.solution_text:
$-15\underset{\sim}{a}+6\underset{\sim}{b}=-3(5\underset{\sim}{a}-2\underset{\sim}{b})$
The second vector is $-3$ times the first, so this pair is parallel.

questions.question_text: Let $\underset{\sim}{p}=\begin{pmatrix}-16\\24\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{q}=\begin{pmatrix}10\\-15\end{pmatrix}$. Which statement correctly determines whether they are parallel?

options.text: They are not parallel because the scalar $-\frac{5}{8}$ is negative.
options.why: Rejects a negative scalar, although a non-zero negative scalar still gives parallel vectors.

options.text: They are not parallel because no whole number $k$ gives $\underset{\sim}{q}=k\underset{\sim}{p}$.
options.why: Assumes the scalar must be a whole number; the non-zero scalar $-\frac{5}{8}$ works in both components.
Drops the sign change: $\frac{5}{8}\underset{\sim}{p}=\begin{pmatrix}-10\\15\end{pmatrix}$, which is not $\underset{\sim}{q}$.

questions.question_text:
The vectors $\begin{pmatrix}4\\h\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}-12\\27\end{pmatrix}$ are parallel.
Find the value of $h$.

options.why: Found $k=3$ from the sizes of the first components and lost the sign change.
Multiplied $27$ by $k=-3$ instead of dividing by it.
Multiplied instead of dividing and also lost the sign change.

questions.question_text: For which values of $s$ are $\begin{pmatrix}s\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}8\\s\end{pmatrix}$ parallel?

options.why: Solved $s^{2}=16$ but kept only the positive square root, although $s=-4$ also works.
Reached $s^{2}=16$ and then read off $s$ without taking the square root.
Subtracted the known components, $8-2$, instead of multiplying them.

questions.question_text: Given $\underset{\sim}{u}=4\underset{\sim}{i}-\underset{\sim}{j}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=\underset{\sim}{i}+2\underset{\sim}{j}$, find the value of $m$ for which $\underset{\sim}{u}+m\underset{\sim}{v}$ is parallel to $\underset{\sim}{i}+\underset{\sim}{j}$.

options.why: Set each component equal to $1$ rather than equal to each other, solving $4+m=1$.
Subtracted $m\underset{\sim}{v}$ instead of adding it, solving $4-m=-1-2m$.
Made the vector parallel to $\underset{\sim}{i}-\underset{\sim}{j}$, solving $4+m=-(-1+2m)$.

questions.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{u}+m\underset{\sim}{v}=(4+m)\underset{\sim}{i}+(-1+2m)\underset{\sim}{j}$
For this to be parallel to $\underset{\sim}{i}+\underset{\sim}{j}$ the two components must be equal.
$4+m=-1+2m$
$5=m$
$m=5$

questions.question_text: Which vector is not parallel to $\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\end{pmatrix}$?

options.why: Rejects an opposite-direction multiple as not parallel; this is $-1$ times the given vector, so it is parallel.
Rejects a general non-zero scalar multiple as not parallel; the same non-zero scalar $k$ multiplies both components, so it is parallel.
Rejects a fractional multiple as not parallel; this is $\frac{1}{4}$ times the given vector, so it is parallel.

questions.solution_text: Parallel vectors are scalar multiples. The first, third and fourth vectors are multiples of $(4,3)$, but $(3,4)$ is not, so option B is not parallel.
